title: Dinah Washington's brushes and Ray Charles teaching a gospel feel
summary: On What a Difference a Day Makes he used press rolls with brushes; Ray Charles showed him the church quarter-note brush feel for Drown in My Own Tears.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: And then I did "What a Difference a Day Makes" with Dinah Washington. Now that was another one that everyone was talking about the rhythm, and the rhythm on that was the press rolls with the brushes -- that was what that was. Instead of playing like that with the sticks, I played with the brushes. (Demonstrates) And that sold; that was a big hit. And then I did "Drowning in My Own Tears" with Ray Charles. Now that was quite an experience for me, because Ray was the one who pulled my coat how to taught me to play the brushes like in the church, with a Gospel feeling.
And all I played, I'm telling you ...

It is so simple; it is so simple that you wouldn't believe it. All I played was just straight quarter notes. He sang said ... "It brings me tears" -- chat's all I played with those brushes. Because if you remember, in the church, that was the way the mothers used to keep the babies quiet on their knees when they were singing; all they did was lift their foot and then drop it -- just a straight 4-4, that's all they were doing, and the baby, they'd be patting the baby and they'd go right back to sleep. And that's what I was playing on the drums with Drowning In My Own Tears." (Demonstrates)
Yeah, he suggested it, and showed me how to do it, too; he came over to the drums and showed me how it was done, and I did it, and I was really thrilled about that.
